title: Respiratory System
shortDescription: The full air pathway from nose to alveoli, the two lungs, the diaphragm, and how gas exchange actually happens.
genZNote: One straight pipe from your nose to a bunch of tiny balloons — that's the whole chapter.

illustration.alt: Labelled illustration of the lungs, trachea, bronchi, and diaphragm
illustration.caption: Lungs (Respiratory System) — Cellfie Human Anatomy

structures.name: Trachea
structures.description: The windpipe; a tube reinforced with cartilage rings, below the larynx.
structures.function: Carries air from the larynx down toward the bronchi.

structures.name: Right bronchus
structures.description: Branch of the trachea entering the right lung.
structures.function: Shorter, wider, and more vertical than the left bronchus.
structures.highYield: Its shape is why inhaled foreign objects more often lodge in the right lung.

structures.name: Left bronchus
structures.description: Branch of the trachea entering the left lung.
structures.function: Carries air into the left lung; narrower and more angled than the right.

structures.name: Bronchioles
structures.description: Progressively smaller branching airways inside each lung.
structures.function: Distribute air deep into the lung tissue toward the alveoli.

structures.name: Alveoli
structures.description: Tiny grape-like air sacs at the end of the bronchioles.
structures.function: Site of gas exchange between air and blood.
structures.highYield: Their huge combined surface area and thin walls (one cell thick) are what make efficient gas exchange possible.

structures.name: Diaphragm
structures.description: Dome-shaped muscle beneath the lungs, separating the thoracic and abdominal cavities.
structures.function: Contracts and flattens to draw air into the lungs (inhalation); relaxes to help push air out (exhalation).

structures.name: Right lung
structures.description: The larger of the two lungs.
structures.function: Divided into three lobes; site of gas exchange on the right side.

structures.name: Left lung
structures.description: The smaller of the two lungs.
structures.function: Divided into two lobes, leaving room for the heart.

comparisons.distinction: The right lung has three lobes and is larger; the left lung has two lobes, leaving space for the heart.
Bronchi are the larger branching airways right after the trachea; bronchioles are their much smaller, more numerous continuations.

questions.prompt: In the labelled respiratory illustration, where does actual gas exchange with the blood take place?
questions.explanation: Alveoli are the tiny air sacs where oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged with the surrounding capillaries.
optionNotes: Just an air passageway, no gas exchange occurs here.
Still a large airway, only conducts air.
A muscle that drives breathing, not a gas-exchange site.

questions.prompt: The diaphragm belongs primarily to which system's mechanics, even though it's a muscle?
questions.explanation: Although it is a muscle, the diaphragm's contraction and relaxation directly drive inhalation and exhalation, making it central to respiratory mechanics.
optionNotes: It's muscle tissue, but its featured role here is driving breathing.
Sits near, but is not part of, the digestive tract.

questions.prompt: Which airway is wider, shorter, and more vertical — making it the more common site for an inhaled foreign object to lodge?
questions.explanation: The right bronchus is shorter, wider, and more vertically aligned with the trachea than the left, so inhaled objects are statistically more likely to end up there.
optionNotes: The left bronchus is narrower and more angled.
The trachea is the main windpipe before it branches, not a bronchus.
The larynx is the voice box, above the trachea.

sections.heading: Structures of the Airway
bullets: Nose / nasal cavity — filters, warms, and humidifies incoming air.
Pharynx — shared passage for air and food.
Larynx — the voice box; also directs air into the trachea and food into the esophagus.
Trachea — the windpipe; a rigid tube reinforced with cartilage rings.
Bronchi — the trachea splits into a right and left bronchus, one per lung.
Bronchioles — smaller branching airways inside each lung.
Alveoli — tiny air sacs at the end of the bronchioles, the actual site of gas exchange.

sections.heading: Lungs and the Diaphragm
sections.body: The right lung has three lobes and the left lung has two (making room for the heart). The diaphragm is the dome-shaped muscle beneath the lungs; it contracts and flattens during inhalation, expanding the chest cavity, and relaxes during exhalation.

sections.heading: Air Pathway
sections.body: Nose → nasal cavity → pharynx → larynx → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli.

sections.heading: Gas Exchange and Transport
bullets: Inspiration — diaphragm and intercostal muscles contract, chest volume increases, air flows in.
Expiration — diaphragm relaxes, chest volume decreases, air flows out.
Gas exchange — oxygen diffuses from alveoli into the surrounding capillaries; carbon dioxide diffuses the opposite way, from blood into the alveoli to be exhaled.
Oxygen is carried in the blood mainly bound to hemoglobin in red blood cells; most carbon dioxide travels as bicarbonate ion in the plasma.

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: The respiratory system moves air along a branching pathway to the alveoli, where oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged with the blood.
keyFacts: Air pathway: nose → nasal cavity → pharynx → larynx → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli.
Right lung has 3 lobes; left lung has 2 (to accommodate the heart).
Gas exchange happens only at the alveoli, not in the trachea or bronchi.
The diaphragm contracting causes inhalation, not exhalation.
commonConfusion: Pharynx (shared air/food passage) is often confused with larynx (voice box, air only, below the pharynx).
Diaphragm contraction = inhalation, not exhalation — a frequently reversed exam fact.

highYieldFacts: The right lung has three lobes, the left has two — asymmetry caused by the heart's position.
Alveoli are the only site of gas exchange in the entire respiratory tract.
commonTraps: Don't place gas exchange at the bronchi or trachea — only the alveoli (and their surrounding capillaries) exchange gases.
The trachea splits into bronchi, not directly into bronchioles.
mustRemember: Full air pathway: nose → nasal cavity → pharynx → larynx → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli.
Oxygen travels bound to hemoglobin; carbon dioxide travels mostly as bicarbonate.
